task: Order seeds and plan this year's crop rotation
Check stored onions, potatoes & squash; remove any rot
Prepare beds and add compost once the snow's gone and soil is workable
Harden off hardy seedlings (onions, brassicas) on the sheltered deck
Watch the forecast — frost is still likely here
Greenhouse: harden off seedlings and grow on early sowings
Chit seed potatoes on a bright, cool sill (10–15°C) for a few weeks before planting
Force rhubarb under a bucket once the buds show
Keep fleece handy for late frosts
Mulch beds to lock in moisture
Harden off tender seedlings on the sheltered deck before planting out after the last frost
Side-shoot tomatoes and feed weekly
Hoe weeds while they're still small
Water deeply in dry spells
Dry and store lifted garlic somewhere airy
Greenhouse: damp down the paths in hot weather
Order garlic and overwintering onion sets
Greenhouse: strip lower tomato leaves for airflow and ripening
Cure onions fully before storing
Move tender pots into the frost-free conservatory before the first frost
Clear spent crops and add them to the compost
Mulch bare beds or sow green manure
Lift hardy roots (carrots, beetroot, parsnips) into sand boxes before the freeze
Mulch and fleece overwintering garlic and onions
Drain and store hoses and water butts before they freeze and crack
Plan the four-year crop rotation and pick a patch to green-manure this year.
Test germination of older saved seed on damp paper towel before ordering new seed.
Dig heavy clay soil in autumn and leave the clods rough so frost breaks them up.
Dig light sandy soil in spring, only shallowly, working in manure or compost at the same time.
Prepare seedbeds once the soil is workable: rake fine and remove weed roots.
Do a spade test in moist summer soil: check roots, crumb structure and earthworms.
If soil pH is below 5.5, spread dolomite lime at half dose, a month apart from manuring.
Spread well-rotted manure, at most 3 kg per m² in two doses, and work it in shallowly.
Spread fresh manure on clay soil in autumn and work it in.
Mix a rich potting compost of manure, compost, sand and meals; store it cool over winter.
Make sand-and-grass-clipping potting mix in sealed black sacks; usable after two months.
Spread mature compost on beds and work it into the topsoil.
Spread half-rotted compost on beds in autumn so it matures by spring.
Turn the garden compost into the empty bay, cover it and leave it to mature for a year.
Cover the garden compost heap when it is about a metre high and water it in dry spells.
Empty the kitchen compost bin before the cold arrives so it can be filled all winter.
Fill sacks with dry leaves or sawdust as compost bulking material and store them frost-free.
Keep the winter kitchen compost going: extra insulating lid or straw, add bulking material, stir often.
Collect fallen leaves in a mesh or wooden bin for leaf mould; turn after a year.
Bury bokashi stored over winter 40 cm deep once the ground thaws; plant 2–3 weeks later.
Sow green manure densely as soon as the soil is workable and keep it moist.
Sow a green manure catch crop on beds cleared of early crops.
Cut annual green manure before it sets seed and dig it in shallowly.
Dig in late-summer-sown and perennial green manure shallowly in spring.
Cut vigorous green manure two or three times and spread the clippings between rows.
Mulch beds and raised beds for winter with leaves, straw, hay or plant waste, only a little fresh grass.
Rake off what remains of the winter mulch so the sun can warm the soil.
Mulch 5–10 cm between rows once seedlings are up, and straight after planting out.
Top up mulch with 5 cm fresh grass clippings as it breaks down; stop adding fresh green after July.
Make a stale seedbed: prepare it, wait 1–2 weeks, rake shallowly to kill weeds, then sow.
Hoe weeds regularly from first emergence and cut off weed seed heads; ease off in late summer.
Clear perennial weeds by repeatedly hoeing and removing every root, starting the autumn before sowing.
Smother perennial weeds by covering ground with cardboard or black fabric under mulch, spring to spring.
Thin direct sowings when seedlings are a few cm tall, in one or two rounds.
Loosen crusted soil with a cultivator, especially early in the season and after heavy rain.
Check soil moisture with a trowel and water thoroughly, about 30 litres per m², preferably in the morning.
Top-dress hungry crops with liquid feed or fresh grass clippings; never feed in late summer or autumn.
Brew nettle or comfrey liquid feed for 10–14 days, dilute to weak tea and use weekly.
Work wood ash into the soil, about 1 kg per m², especially around berry bushes.
Liquid-feed container plants weekly, starting 3–4 weeks after planting.
Mulch pots and check they are moist right through, especially before going on holiday.
Repot overwintered perennials in containers into fresh soil mixed with compost and manure.
Give indoor seedlings grow lights 14–16 hours a day, keep them at 12–18°C and air covers daily.
Prick out seedlings into individual pots of rich soil once the first true leaves appear.
Harden off indoor-raised plants over a week before planting them out.
Cover new sowings and transplants with fleece for a couple of weeks for even moisture and shelter.
Keep carrots, onions and brassicas under well-anchored fleece or mesh until harvest against flies and caterpillars.
Protect brassica and radish seedlings from flea beetles with fleece until they have 4–6 leaves.
Check brassica leaf undersides for butterfly eggs and caterpillars; crush or hand-pick them.
Protect pea and bean sowings from birds with fleece or spruce twigs.
Hunt slugs at dusk or dawn, empty beer traps daily and water in the morning.
Hose aphids off with cold water; if needed spray soap solution weekly, not in sunshine.
Spray potatoes and tomatoes with salicylic acid at 20–25 cm tall, repeating after 1–2 weeks, against blight.
Trample snow around fruit bushes and trees to deter voles; keep the ground around them bare.
Cover pots with bubble-wrap hoods on frosty nights to extend the season.
Overwinter perennials in pots: sink them in a bed or compost, or pack them in an insulated box by a wall.
Clean, dry and sharpen tools, oil metal parts and treat handles with linseed oil and turpentine.
Lift pallet-collar frames off the beds and store them under cover for winter.
Empty containers used for annuals, rinse and store them dry; spread the old soil on beds.
Choose and mark the best, most typical plants for seed, at least five, and give them extra space.
Tie fleece bags over flowers of plants grown for seed before they open to prevent crossing.
Harvest ripe seed in dry weather; before frost or autumn rain pull plants and dry them indoors.
Clean and dry saved seed, then store it dry, cool and dark over winter.
Lift biennials chosen for seed and store them cool and frost-free for replanting in spring.
Replant overwintered biennial roots and plants to flower and set seed.
At harvest, select long smooth parsnip, salsify and scorzonera roots and replant them for seed.
Leave the best pea and broad bean pods until dry and rattling, then dry indoors and shell.
Save seed from overripe tomatoes (ferment and rinse) and chillies (scrape out and dry).
Cut seeding lettuce after the first frost, hang it indoors to dry, then thresh the seed.
Start new beds in autumn: dig, weed and mulch so worms improve the soil over winter.
Cut flexible withies and build plant supports on site once the bed is prepared.
Feed hungry crops in deep beds with liquid feed every other week unless mulched with fresh grass clippings.
Dig a trench down the middle of deep beds and fill it with leaves and weeds, or mulch the beds.
In early spring rake off undecomposed mulch from deep beds, dig one spit deep and work in compost and manure.
Sow fast cold-hardy crops for autumn harvest and keep transplants ready to fill any bed space that empties.
Build a compost loaf from branches, turf, clippings, compost and soil, then cover it with black plastic or straw.
Use fleece as frost protection on cold spring and autumn nights.
Keep fleece over pest-prone crops all season with edges anchored; remove it the last one to two weeks before harvest.
Open both ends of plastic growing tunnels in midsummer and lift the side when watering.
Put up a mobile plastic tunnel over cold-hardy crops to extend harvest into late autumn.
Tend cold frames: ventilate daily with a wedge, shade seedlings at midday, cover with a mat on frosty nights.
Extend the cold greenhouse season: seal gaps, repair panes, add bubble wrap and fleece, run a heater above 6°C.
Remove the plastic from a tunnel greenhouse for winter, or anchor it well with stones or sandbags.
Fill greenhouse containers with fresh potting soil in spring and empty the old soil onto vegetable beds in autumn.
Replace the top layer of greenhouse bed soil each spring with compost; change all soil every two to three years.
Mulch greenhouse sand beds with 10 cm fresh grass clippings, adding another 10 cm a month later.
Ventilate the greenhouse daily, especially in the afternoon so no condensation forms overnight.
Shade the sunniest side of the greenhouse on hot days with shade cloth, fleece or old lace curtains.
Water greenhouse plants in the morning, shower them on hot days and mulch to keep moisture.
Inspect greenhouse plants regularly, crush egg clusters and start biological pest control early in the season.
Clean the greenhouse thoroughly after the season: clear debris, wash pots, hose down and scrub with soap solution.
Sow slow-germinating crops in a weeded, fed bed just before the ground freezes, covering seed with sandy soil.
Cover autumn-sown beds with fleece in spring to speed up emergence.
Sow fast leafy greens in the tunnel greenhouse or cold frame in late autumn for harvest before tomatoes go in.
For a hot bed, dig a 30-50 cm pit, fill it with straw against frost, and store dry leaves.
Build a hot bed of fresh horse manure and straw; add soil at 50°C, sow at 20°C.
Ventilate the hot bed daily, cover it at night, lift the window above 30°C; reuse spent straw as mulch.
Grow microgreens and baby leaves indoors under grow lights during the darkest months.
Bring a few chilli, tomato or herb plants indoors to a sunny window to keep harvesting into winter.
Store potatoes and root crops cool and dark, ideally in a 1-4°C cellar; watch the thermometer for balcony storage boxes.
Lift root crops just before frost, top and dry them, and pack them into a newspaper-lined buried cement-ring cellar.
Build a straw-covered clamp for roots and potatoes; add the soil layer only when frost threatens.
Insulate clamps and mini-cellars with leaves or spruce branches and open them only briefly in mild weather.
Work compost into the herb bed every year to keep the soil light and well drained.
Feed perennial herbs sparingly, e.g. 5 cm of grass clippings at the start of the season; avoid excess nitrogen.
Weed and hoe the herb bed and water perennial herbs only in extreme drought.
Hose aphids off lemon balm and tarragon with a hard jet of water and crush egg clusters.
Cut herbaceous perennial herbs right down in late spring once new shoots appear from the base.
Cut woody herbs back by about half in late spring, never into old wood; do not cut back in autumn.
Cut oregano down to 5-7 cm, wormwood to 15 cm and trim rue in spring.
Cover tender perennial herbs with spruce branches in late autumn; never use leaves that mat down.
Lay fleece over thyme and other woody herbs in late winter to shield them from burning sun and frost swings.
Renew perennial herbs every three to six years by dividing them in spring and replanting with compost.
Take 10 cm tip cuttings of herbs, or peg down layers, to propagate them.
Collect ripe dry herb seed; sow perennial herbs in a fleece-covered box left outdoors over winter.
Harvest herbs just before flowering and dry them in small hanging bunches somewhere airy and dark.
Bring potted rosemary, lemongrass, lemon verbena and basil indoors before frost; keep bright, cool and barely watered.
In spring trim dead leaves, repot and divide lemongrass and prune lemon verbena before moving them outside.
Cut basil back to two or three leaf pairs once it has six to eight, to delay flowering; keep feeding.
Cut lemon balm back by half after the midsummer harvest and cut lovage down once it turns scruffy.
Cut off sweet cicely seed heads to stop it spreading and trim spignel into a ball after flowering.
Watch for self-sown herb seedlings when weeding and keep mint in check with a spade.
Feed berry bushes only in spring, with bone meal, wood ash or manure; late feeding stops shoots ripening for winter.
Water berry plants generously while berries develop, mulch, and never water in the evening.
Weed under berry bushes diligently and keep the soil open or mulched.
Cover flowering berry bushes with fleece on frosty nights and water before frost.
Protect ripening berries from birds with nets or a scarecrow; put red-painted walnuts in the strawberry bed.
Take cuttings of currants and gooseberries (20 cm) and sea buckthorn (10-15 cm) and root them in sand.
Mulch arctic bramble over winter and rake the cover away in spring.
Cut out blackberry and tayberry canes that have fruited after harvest.
Lay first-year blackberry and tayberry canes on the ground and cover them with spruce branches or straw.
Fan-train last year's blackberry canes on wires, thin to six to eight, and cut back dead tips.
Feed blueberries in spring and again as flowering starts; mulch with acidic conifer litter.
Prune established blueberries and saskatoons by removing about a fifth of the oldest and drooping branches.
Feed raspberries with up to 2 kg manure per metre and mulch with clippings mixed with leaves or straw.
Keep the raspberry row weeded and pull up suckers coming up outside the row.
Right after harvest cut fruited raspberry canes to the ground and thin new canes to about ten per metre.
Top raspberry canes taller than 170 cm and cut out and burn canes with gall midge swellings.
Cut all autumn raspberry canes to the ground after harvest.
Shake raspberry beetles into a bucket of soapy water early each morning while raspberries flower.
Keep fleece over strawberries until the first flowers open to protect buds from strawberry blossom weevil.
Keep strawberry beds unmulched until fruits hang down, then put straw between the rows.
Water strawberries in the morning during fruiting and remove damaged or mouldy berries.
Feed strawberries after harvest and cut off the foliage if the bed is diseased.
Cut off strawberry runners not needed for new plants.
Renew strawberry beds every three to four years on a new site using rooted runners planted by late summer.
Winter-cover strawberry beds with straw, dry leaves or fleece.
Spray wild strawberries with soapy water before flowering against strawberry leaf beetle.
Thin established bushes: remove drooping and damaged branches and the three or four oldest stems at the base.
Watch for gooseberry sawfly larvae and pick or shake them off before they strip the bush.
Spray aphid-blistered red currants with soapy water; dig up and burn black currants with swollen gall-mite buds.
On espaliered or standard currants and gooseberries, cut out the oldest branches and tie in young ones.
Rake up and remove fallen lingonberry leaves spotted by leaf-fall disease.
